title: What if the harness mattered more than the model? - Aditya Bhargava, Etsy

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's central thesis is that harness architecture matters more than model capability, demonstrated through agent loops, multi-agent patterns, and control-plane design. Agency is a developer-facing language for building agents, and all demonstrations use coding agent examples. Agency is described as 6 months into development with no prior tools meeting the speaker's needs. Prerequisites include TypeScript, Python, LLM tool calling, and functional programming familiarity. summary: Aditya Bhargava (Etsy Staff Engineer, IC initiative lead for Agentic Commerce, author of Grokking Algorithms) presents his thesis that harnesses matter more than models. The industry wisdom says models are so good you can keep harnesses simple, but he argues this creates reliance on proprietary models that can't run locally. He cites the Harness Bench paper: 106 tasks, same model and evaluation, only the harness changed—scores ranged from 52.4% to 76.2%, over 20 points difference. For weaker models, the harness matters more, which is great news because any developer can build harnesses. He argues building a good harness requires language-level support, leading him to build Agency, a new language for building agents (6 months in, inspired by TypeScript with Python syntax). Terminology: agent = harness + model. The talk demonstrates building a coding agent across seven examples fixing a buggy median function. Example 1: bare LLM call can't read/write files. Example 2: every function automatically becomes a tool with auto-generated JSON schema. Example 3: interrupts pause execution for human approval on destructive/sensitive operations. Example 4: partial function application (PFA) locks the directory parameter so the agent can only read/write within demo—safe without human input. Example 5: the ReAct pattern (reason, act, observe, loop) gives the agent a feedback loop to run tests, observe failures, modify code, and confirm success. Example 6: sub-agents—the main agent uses a coding agent and a Wikipedia agent as tools, running them in parallel; sub-agents add capabilities without bloating context. Example 7: self-optimization via Agency's built-in Japa optimizer, which marks variables with an optimize modifier, establishes a baseline (0.2 objective), and systematically rewrites prompts to improve—moving from guess-and-check to measured improvement. Agency's language-level support includes simple tool syntax, interrupts/handlers/PFA for safety, true pause-and-resume execution (can pause inside loops, tool calls, or sub-agents, serialize, and resume a week later), and built-in optimizers. Main takeaways: agent = model + harness; better harness equals better performance, especially for weaker models; build better harnesses by adding tools, safety, autonomy, reasoning, sub-agents, and self-optimization.

sections.title: Introduction and Controversial Thesis
sections.summary: Aditya Bhargava introduces himself (Etsy Staff Engineer, Grokking Algorithms author). His controversial take: the industry wisdom that models are good enough to keep harnesses simple is moving in the wrong direction, creating reliance on proprietary models. He advocates focusing on open-source local models with harnesses good enough to match cutting-edge performance.

sections.title: Harness Bench Evidence and Agency Language Introduction
sections.summary: Cites Harness Bench paper: 106 tasks, same model/evaluation, only harness changed—52.4% to 76.2% range, 20+ point difference. For weaker models, harness matters more. Argues building good harnesses needs language-level support, introduces Agency, a new language for building agents. Defines terminology: agent = harness + model.

sections.title: Talk Roadmap and Coding Agent Task Setup
sections.summary: Outlines talk goals: basics of building a harness, agent safety, advanced concepts (sub-agents, self-optimization). The coding task: fix a buggy median function in demo/median.py that doesn't correctly handle odd vs. even length lists. Seven examples will show the same agent with progressively improving harness.

sections.title: Example 1: Bare LLM Call
sections.summary: Shows Agency code resembling TypeScript with Python syntax. Entry point node main, simple prompt passed to LLM function. Agent can't read/write files and asks to see the code—bare model with minimal harness fails.

sections.title: Example 2: Tools in Agency
sections.summary: Demonstrates tool mechanics: every function automatically becomes a tool. Agency generates JSON schema, uses doc string as tool description. Shows greet function example and built-in log viewer showing tool calls, parameters, and responses.

sections.title: Interrupts and Human-in-the-Loop Safety
sections.summary: Read/write tools are built into Agency but raise interrupts by default requiring approval. Unhandled interrupts crash with guidance. Handler blocks capture interrupts and prompt users for approval. All standard library functions that mutate, destroy, or read sensitive data throw interrupts. Safe but slow.

sections.title: Example 4: Partial Function Application for Constrained Autonomy
sections.summary: Completes PFA explanation: locking the directory parameter to 'demo' so the agent can only read/write within that directory. The LLM doesn't see the directory argument—only the filename. Run shows agent reads file without asking permission and gives correct solution, but doesn't update the file itself. PFA is a great way to constrain capabilities—safe without human input.

sections.title: Example 5: ReAct Feedback Loop
sections.summary: Introduces the ReAct pattern (reason and act): reason, act, observe consequences, decide next step, loop until tests pass. The agent reads files, runs tests (fail), writes fix, runs tests again (pass). This is a key stage—agent now figures out the task, checks failure, modifies code, and confirms success. Recaps the harness improvement ladder: model → tools → handlers → PFA → feedback loop.

sections.title: Example 6: Sub-Agents for Expanded Capabilities
sections.summary: Introduces sub-agents. Main agent gets two sub-agents as tools instead of read/write: a coding agent (own LLM call, own tools) and a Wikipedia agent (with built-in Wikipedia search tool). In Agency, sub-agents are just functions—consistent with how tools work. Demo runs sub-agents in parallel: coding agent fixes file, Wikipedia agent researches Jensen's inequality, produces a limerick. Sub-agents add capabilities without bloating context; prevents tool-selection confusion by grouping related tools.

sections.title: Example 7: Self-Optimization via Japa Optimizer
sections.summary: Agency has built-in optimizers including Japa. Mark variables with 'optimize' modifier, give optimizer a goal. Two basic prompts optimized against goal 'Fix the bug in median.py using TDD.' Baseline objective 0.2; optimizer rewrites prompts and achieves objective in first iteration. This moves from trial-and-error to systematic, measured improvement. Full optimizer run shown from earlier recording.

sections.title: Harness Improvement Ladder Recap
sections.summary: Recaps the full ladder: nothing (model alone), tools (unsafe), handlers (safe but slow), PFA (safe and fast), reasoning/feedback loop (higher confidence), sub-agents (more capabilities), self-optimization (measured improvement). Invites audience to experiment with building better harnesses to enable local models.

sections.title: Agency Language-Level Support and Conclusion
sections.summary: Lists Agency's language-level support: simple tool syntax, safety via interrupts/handlers/PFA, true pause-and-resume execution (can pause inside loops, tool calls, sub-agents; serialize and resume even a week later without code changes—a rare feature), built-in optimizers. Install via npm. Main takeaways: agent = model + harness; better harness = better performance especially for weaker models; build better harnesses with tools, safety, autonomy, reasoning, sub-agents, self-optimization. Points to agencylang.com and Blue Sky.
